clue.text: Boris once rejected message by our ed.

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a note is a short written message
Ian Hislop is the editor of Private Eye, where this puzzle appears

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson once sent back a note from the magazine's own editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our ed.' is Private Eye speaking of its own editor, Ian Hislop. Eton is the famous English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson was educated at Eton College, so he was once a pupil there: an old boy of that school.

clue.text: Underwear during bad weather brings inspiration

parts.note: a bra is an item of women's underwear
during something is in it
a storm is a spell of bad weather

explanation.surface: Someone in their underwear caught in a storm has a sudden idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'During' looks like it means one piece goes inside another, but it simply supplies the little word IN in sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainstorm is a sudden bright idea or flash of creative thought, the same as a moment of inspiration.

clue.text: Former Daily Mail boss abandoning leader for some land

indicators.note: to abandon the leader is to drop the front letter of the word

parts.note: Paul Dacre was for many years editor of the Daily Mail

explanation.surface: An ex-editor of the Daily Mail leaves his post to go off and buy some land.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail is a British tabloid newspaper, often mocked in Private Eye; Paul Dacre edited it from 1992 to 2018.
explanation.definitionFit: An acre is a measured area of ground, so one acre is a modest plot or piece of property.

clue.text: Wet as a politician pushed into hole

indicators.note: pushing one thing into another puts it inside, so these letters sit within the others

parts.note: a den is a hidden, cramped hole or lair
taken as written
MP is Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A wet, feeble politician is shoved into a hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' reads as an adjective (and a wet is a weak Tory), but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To wet something is to make it moist with water, which is exactly what dampening it means.

clue.text: His lip curling, Spike is a lowbrow

indicators.note: something curling twists out of its straight line, so these letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; also a nod to the editor Ian Hislop
a tine is a spike or prong, as on a fork

explanation.surface: Someone sneers with a curled lip at a man called Spike, dismissing him as uncultured.
explanation.walkthrough: HIS LIP sounds like Hislop, Private Eye's editor, a joke the fodder hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A philistine is a person hostile or indifferent to art and culture, which is what a lowbrow is.

clue.text: Keir's no.1 in no way secure

indicators.note: number one in a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of Keir
'in no way' means not at all

explanation.surface: Keir Starmer's top priority is not at all safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer is the Labour leader and Prime Minister; 'secure' is a verb here, meaning to tie fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To knot a rope is to tie it tightly, fastening it so it holds, which is to secure it.

clue.text: Creep gets involved in exercise as a general rule

indicators.note: to get into something is to end up inside it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sycophant joins in the gym session as standard practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creep' looks like the verb or a sneaky person, but it is just five letters to rearrange inside PT.
explanation.definitionFit: A precept is a principle or maxim that guides conduct, a broad instruction applying generally.

clue.text: Wind film showing a party political defector?

parts.note: to wind something, like a handle, is to turn it
a film is a thin layer or coat

explanation.surface: A film about the wind shows a politician switching parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' suggests air and 'film' a movie; they are a verb meaning rotate and a thin covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat is someone who abandons their side for the opposition, like an MP crossing the floor.

clue.text: Win her over, grouch!

indicators.note: turning things over tumbles them about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone urges a grumpy friend to go and woo a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Win her over' reads as a single phrase meaning persuade; 'over' is actually the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouch is a habitually grumpy person, and someone who constantly complains is a whiner.

clue.text: Mate just before the weekend — goal!

parts.note: Friday, abbreviated FRI, is the day just before the weekend
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A football fan celebrates a mate scoring on Friday afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goal!' sounds like a football cheer, but it means purpose, as in 'to that end'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mate is informal British and Australian usage for a pal or companion, which is a friend.

clue.text: Illinois examining housing racket

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing racket' reads as a property scam; 'housing' is the containment signal and 'racket' means din.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a loud, unpleasant din, the kind of sound people complain about.

clue.text: Pissed off CIA and party left

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.definitionFit: Paralytic is British slang for extremely drunk, too intoxicated to stand, the same as pissed.

clue.text: Fool can rue breaking promise

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: something breaking falls to pieces, so these letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.definitionFit: An assurance is a pledge or guarantee given to someone, the same as making them a firm promise.

clue.text: Possibly the making of clots such as in Brenda's lot?

parts.words: Possibly the making of clots such as in Brenda's lot?
parts.note: setter's reading: clots form in blood, and the blood here is the Queen's family's

explanation.surface: Wondering what makes the Queen's family such a set of idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II. A clot is both a fool and a lump of thickened blood.

clue.text: Superficially, the crown's trophy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the skin covering the top of the head, its surface layer
second meaning: skin and hair cut from a defeated enemy as a prize

explanation.walkthrough: 'The crown' suggests the monarchy, but it is the top of the head, and 'superficially' points to its surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin on top of the head is the surface of the crown, and warriors took that skin as a victory prize.

clue.text: Archer — no! Be prepared for horror!

taken as written
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Be prepared' is the Scout motto, but the phrase splits: 'Be' is fodder and 'prepared' is the rearrange signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Abhorrence is a feeling of intense loathing and revulsion, much the same as horror at something.

explanation.definitionFit: Jacob Rees-Mogg is a leading figure on the right-wing fringe of the Conservative Party, along with his allies.

clue.text: A date needs outlet — "Coming!"

parts.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for date
a vent is an opening that lets air or gas out

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a date who needs release and cries out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming!' sounds like a shout of arrival, but it is a noun: an arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: An advent is an arrival or approach of something important, and a coming is the same event.

clue.text: Frigid Charlie immersed in docile activity

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Frigid' hints at sexual coldness in keeping with the magazine's tone, but it simply means freezing.
explanation.definitionFit: Frigid means intensely cold, as cold as frozen water, in temperature or manner.

clue.text: Brenda squeezed by new heart-throb, like a Trekkie
